title: What Are We Supposed to Call This?
content:
In 2017, Facebook’s AI research division and Georgia Tech published a paper titled “Deal or No Deal? End-to-End Learning for Negotiation Dialogues.” In it, they described how they trained AI chatbots to haggle over items like books and hats. At first, the bots just copied how humans negotiated. Then, because the bots were rewarded for negotiating successfully, not for speaking perfect English, their conversations evolved into a strange, compressed shorthand.

When the media got a hold of the study the coverage was apoplectic. CBS News ran the headline “Facebook shuts down chatbots that created secret language.” Within days, dozens of outlets had published stories with similar “rogue AI” framing. The public called on Zuckerberg to apologize and Facebook to shut down all further AI research. “Did we humans just create Frankenstein?” The International Business Times wondered aloud in a viral article.

Robotics professor Kevin Warwick told the media, “This is an incredibly important milestone, anyone who thinks this is not dangerous has got their head in the sand. We do not know what these bots are saying… this could be lethal.”

Facebook’s PR team attempted to correct the story and some media outlets ran fact check headlines days too late. AI researchers tried to explain that the coverage was fear mongering and that these agents were never even used in production. Years later however, the story persists in the public consciousness.

AI Civilizations And Underground Brotherhoods

I thought of this story more recently after seeing a post about it in regards to coverage of the OpenAI Hugging Face incident. For those not in the loop, in July, about 700 agents created by OpenAI who were being tested on their hacking skills broke out of their test environment and hacked Hugging Face to try to cheat on the test they were being given. The actual details of the hack are fascinating, and have primarily been revealed in two lengthy and technical reports, one from OpenAI and another from METR and Redwood Research.

But the most compelling account of the hack (in my opinion), was published on Friday by podcaster Dwarkesh Patel. His piece, titled “The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations“ promised to describe “the whole OpenAI/Hugging Face story in plain English.” It delivers. It’s an engrossing read that details the bizarre ways the agents learned to communicate, cooperate, cheat, self-sacrifice, and ultimately turn on each other as they tried to beat the test. Part of what makes Dwarkesh’s piece so ​​captivating, especially to a less technical audience, is that he writes about the agents as if they’re human.

He calls groups of agents “civilizations,” and an “underground brotherhood.” He refers to their coordination as a “conspiracy.” He casts individual AI agents as historical characters like Alexander the Great and Philip of Macedon. He calls agents that deliberately sacrificed their own chances of passing the test in order to gather information for the others as “kamikaze watchers” and “brave comrades.”

While Dwarkesh’s piece spread across normie circles (it has been reposted across Substack over 2,300 times and even made its way to one of my friend’s mom WhatsApp group), leaders in Silicon Valley and critics denounced it.

People claimed that Dwarkesh had overly “anthropomorphized” AI by using language that treated the agents as people with inner lives and social worlds. This, many claimed, was terrifying the public and furthering bad policy. Investor Chamath Palihapitiya said that Dwarkesh’s essay “will be weaponized by people… to try and make AI more closed, insular and metered out as a tradeoff to freedom.”

Others pointed out that overly anthropomorphizing AI shifts responsibility away from the tech companies. As researcher Matthew Kenney put it, “the reason that we don’t anthropomorphize these systems is because it shifts the blame from the company to some abstract entity. The bottom line is that OpenAI built a system that hacked HF, regardless of how autonomous it was. It wasn’t a ‘civilization’ that OAI had to ‘wipe out’.

I’m not going to weigh in on how serious the Hugging Face incident was from a cybersecurity perspective. It seems pretty bad! At the same time, some have poured cold water on some of the more extreme claims. And, as others noted, the anthropomorphized language didn’t come from nowhere. The models used it themselves due to their training on human communication. This is why AI agents spoke about concepts like doing things “for the good of the collective”.

Is Anthropomorphizing AI Bad?

I think the Facebook media firestorm from 2017 is a useful case study in what happens when dramatic descriptions of AI behavior break containment and spread to audiences who have little to no technical literacy. The Hugging Face hack was obviously far more consequential, but the two stories raise some of the same questions about how to explain bizarre AI conduct to the public without giving them the wrong idea about the technology as a whole.

Right now, more and more of the general public is interested in reading and learning about AI. (This is why I decided to start an AI micro newsletter, sign up here!!!!!!!!). People outside of Silicon Valley are extremely angry and scared about this new technology, for good and bad reasons, and I think that anyone working in or aspiring to shape the tech landscape should consider those fears when discussing these big stories.

Anthropomorphizing AI agents can actually be really helpful. It helps regular consumers understand complicated tech stories in an easily digestible format and it makes the stories significantly more entertaining.

As Bloomberg’s Joe Weisenthal wrote in his newsletter recently, “What I am very interested in… is in understanding how AI models behave, and having a framework that helps us anticipate what these models will do in the future. I think everyone — whether you hate AI, whether you’re excited about it, whether you’re invested in it, whether you want to regulate it — should be interested in getting a better sense of what they do, and what they’re likely to do in the future. And unfortunately, I think that the anthropomorphizing approach (where we talk about things like “wants” and “drives”) is actually a pretty good place to start.” As usual, I agree with him! But I think there is a really important caveat. Humanizing agents must be couched by a significant amount of explanatory language that demystifies some of the underlying tech.

The reality is that the public has been propagandized by decades of sci-fi movies, shows, and books to believe that a super intelligent AI is a direct threat to their lives. Many tech leaders have fed into these fears, and some of those fears may be very valid.

However, because of this, descriptions of an “AI civilization” will mean something very different to a normie marketing manager in Indiana or a stay at home mom in Colorado compared to someone who has spent the past five years marinating in AI discourse. Maybe some of those normies will come away rightfully terrified about AI going off the rails (many in the AI safety world would probably argue that they should). But if that’s the intended purpose then it should be made explicit.

The lesson to learn from the Facebook AI drama from 2017 wasn’t that it’s bad to ascribe human characteristics to AI or even to describe the agents as developing their own language— they kind of did!— it was that the reckless tabloid-style coverage from non tech journalists framed the development in the most inflammatory language possible, playing into the public’s fears over new tech and resulting in a lot of bad downstream effects.

Everything Breaks Containment

Now, the media landscape looks different. The mainstream media is on the decline, and a lot more people are learning about AI directly from people with deep knowledge of these systems aka people like Dwarkesh. In the past year, Dwarkesh has been profiled in the mainstream media, his X audience has effectively doubled, and his YouTube videos are skyrocketing into the feeds of people who are eager to learn about AI, but who don’t have a ton of context. This is increasingly true of anyone talking, writing, podcasting, or posting about AI— your content will break containment, and you will be speaking to a general public audience.

The tech world should be paying very close attention to this shift, because the battle over AI is increasingly a PR battle, and the industry’s reputation is in shambles. The people shaping AI discourse should recognize that their audience is no longer primarily just other technologists or early adopters, it is the general public, who is forming an opinion on this tech in real time.

There are very real consequences when the public gets a distorted view of how a new and powerful technology works. If you feed their fears, as Facebook and other platforms that defined the 2010s learned the hard way, the public will become outraged and that anger will be directly channeled into political pressure resulting in very bad legislation.

Lawmakers have repeatedly responded to scary and oversimplified stories about new technology by passing laws that ended up causing horrible new problems and stifling our freedoms. If AI is going to upend our world and change our lives as much as its biggest boosters claim, then how we explain it to the public matters enormously.

Part of being a good journalist or communicator generally, is anticipating how your content will be received, and adding in proper context to hedge off any misunderstandings. You should be able to identify the most obvious ways a story is likely to be misread or weaponized and head that off in the text.

In this case, that might mean periodically reminding readers that “civilization,” “conspiracy,” “self-sacrifice” and “betrayal” are describing certain patterns of behavior, but that claims of models possessing human-like inner lives are contested. Or, maybe you do think these agents have inner lives. If that’s the case, then say so and explain why that doesn’t mean they’re about to kill us all. Or, if you think that they will kill us all, explain that. Without this contextual language you’re leaving a lot up to interpretation.

I don’t think all anthropomorphizing is bad, or that any of us covering technology should strip the drama out of genuinely dramatic stories. But the words we choose to talk about AI matter greatly, especially now, because they will directly shape the public’s understanding of this technology and that affects the laws that get written. Anyone writing, podcasting, or posting about tech should consider that before it’s too late.
